awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of an Automatic Portable Pill Dispenser for Pharmaceutical Compliance
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of an automatic, portable pill dispenser designed to improve medication adherence that advances the national health. This technology is suitable for elderly individuals, patients with chronic conditions, and those with complex medication regimes. Medication non-adherence is reported as the seventh leading cause of death in the U.S., contributing to approximately 125,000 deaths for persons with treatable ailments and up to 25% of hospital readmissions. Additionally, medical non-adherence results in over $500 billion in preventable healthcare costs. These problems are addressable by using an automatic, portable pill dispenser that offers an accessible, patient-centered solution that caregivers can also use in organizing, dispensing, and tracking medication intake more effectively. By reducing the risk of medication error and missing doses, the device aims to lower the frequency of hospital readmission, promote the quality of life of patients, and lower healthcare costs. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. The solution is based on the development of an automated pill dispenser. This technology enables the creation of a highly compact product that remains capable of storing and dispensing multiple different medications. The simple yet effective pill dispensing method fits within the palm of a user’s hand, while including the traditional components of pill dispensers that customers expect. The pill dispensing technology advances the state of the art in medical technology by providing a clever and compact mechanism that is poised for widespread adoption by potential customers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The NSF I-Corps grant focused on customer discovery and prototyping work for an automated pill dispensing technology to help patients manage their daily medication.  Through the NSF I-Corps customer discovery process, 101 interviews with stakeholders across the medication management ecosystem were completed. The customer discovery interviews provided a deep understanding of the market and the real challenges surrounding medication adherence.

Customer discovery enables the identification of customer needs to inform technological development by listening directly to the people most affected by a problem. Through the interview process, caregivers were identified as a key customer segment, since they are often responsible for organizing medications, monitoring adherence, and supporting loved ones through complex treatment plans. Patients were recognized as an additional customer segment making up the primary end users whose daily experiences and outcomes ultimately define the success of any medication management solution.

The customer discovery interviews provided valuable insight into the needs, frustrations, and priorities of both caregivers and patients. By speaking directly with these customer segments, in addition to further stakeholders including healthcare providers and pharmacies, a clearer picture was gained regarding the barriers that contribute to medication nonadherence and the factors that influence whether new technologies are adopted and consistently used. These findings enabled the identification of value propositions that align directly with validated customer needs.  Evidence from interviews played an important role in shaping a Business Model Canvas which focused on aligning value propositions with customer needs, followed by physical prototyping for early product development.

Knowledge gained provided new perspectives for understanding healthcare, caregiving, and pharmacy operations and needs. Insights from patients, caregivers, and pharmacies helped identify factors affecting medication adherence and informed the design of solutions that may reduce medication errors, improve patient outcomes, and support more effective medication management across care settings.  The knowledge directly informs broader impacts for further products for automated pill dispensing with the potential to improve quality of life, promote independent living for aging populations, reduce caregiver stress, and lower healthcare utilization associated with preventable medication related complications.

Ultimately, the customer discovery process resulted in a comprehensive understanding of the healthcare ecosystem and the relationships between caregivers, patients, providers, and pharmacies. The findings provide new insights for improving pill dispensing technologies to directly address real-world customer needs, by ensuring that customer feedback remains at the center of decision-making and future development.
